plain_english: Keep this idea ready: when you lose something external, ask what you gained instead. If what you gained is worth more, never say you suffered a loss. Don't call it a loss if you got a horse instead of a donkey, or an ox instead of a sheep. Don't call it a loss if you did something good instead of making money, or found peace instead of empty chatter, or gained modesty instead of crude talk. Remember this, and you'll always keep your character where it should be.
original_excerpt: Keep this thought in readiness, when you lose anything external, what you acquire in place of it; and if it be worth more, never say, I have had a loss; neither if you have got a horse in place of an ass, or an ox in place of a sheep, nor a good action in place of a bit of money, nor in place of idle talk such tranquillity as befits a man, nor in place of lewd talk if you have acquired modesty. If you remember this, you will always maintain your character such as it ought to be.
source_reference: Discourses, What Things We Should Exchange for Other Things

plain_english: But if you don't, realize that your chances are slipping away. Whatever effort you put into improving yourself will be wasted and destroyed. It takes only small things to lose and destroy everything — just a tiny mistake in thinking. A ship's captain doesn't need much to wreck his vessel. He needs skill and attention to save it, but if he turns it just slightly into the wind, it's lost. Even if he doesn't mean to do this — if he just gets careless for a moment — the ship is lost. The same thing happens here. If you just let your guard down a little, everything you've built up until now is gone.
original_excerpt: But if you do not, consider that the times of opportunity are perishing, and that whatever pains you take about yourself, you are going to waste them all and overturn them. And it needs only a few things for the loss and overturning of all—namely, a small deviation from reason. For the steerer of a ship to upset it, he has no need of the same means as he has need of for saving it; but if he turns it a little to the wind, it is lost; and if he does not do this purposely, but has been neglecting his duty a little, the ship is lost. Something of the kind happens in this case also; if you only fall a nodding a little, all that you have up to this time collected is gone.
source_reference: Discourses, What Things We Should Exchange for Other Things

plain_english: So pay attention to how things appear to you. Watch over your thoughts carefully. What you're trying to protect isn't small stuff. It's your dignity, your honesty, your steady character. It's freedom from wild emotions, a calm mind, freedom from fear, and inner peace. In short — your liberty. What would you sell these things for? Look at what you'd get in exchange. But won't I get something good for it? Look closely. If you do get something back, see what you're really trading for. I have decency — he has a government position. He has high office — I have my dignity. But I don't cheer for things that are wrong. I won't stand when I shouldn't. I'm free, and I'm God's friend. So I obey him willingly.
original_excerpt: Attend therefore to the appearances of things, and watch over them; for that which you have to preserve is no small matter, but it is modesty and fidelity and constancy, freedom from the affects, a state of mind undisturbed, freedom from fear, tranquillity, in a word liberty. For what will you sell these things? See what is the value of the things which you will obtain in exchange for these.—But shall I not obtain any such thing for it?—See, and if you do in return get that, see what you receive in place of it. I possess decency, he possesses a tribuneship: he possesses a prætorship, I possess modesty. But I do not make acclamations where it is not becoming: I will not stand up where I ought not; for I am free, and a friend of God. and so I obey him willingly.
source_reference: Discourses, What Things We Should Exchange for Other Things

plain_english: I must not chase after anything else — not physical health, not possessions, not positions of power, not a good reputation, not anything external. God doesn't want me chasing these things. If he did, he would have made them truly good for me. But he didn't. So I can't go against his commands. Keep what is truly your own good in everything you do. As for everything else, deal with them as circumstances allow, but only as far as reason permits. Be content with this approach alone. If you don't follow this, you'll be miserable. You'll fail at everything. You'll be blocked and frustrated at every turn. These are the laws sent down from above. These are your orders. You should interpret and follow these divine laws — not the legal codes of Masurius and Cassius.
original_excerpt: But I must not claim (seek) anything else, neither body nor possession, nor magistracy, nor good report, nor in fact anything. For he (God) does not allow me to claim (seek) them, for if he had chosen, he would have made them good for me; but he has not done so, and for this reason I cannot transgress his commands. Preserve that which is your own good in everything; and as to every other thing, as it is permitted, and so far as to behave consistently with reason in respect to them, content with this only. If you do not, you will be unfortunate, you will fail in all things, you will be hindered, you will be impeded. These are the laws which have been sent from thence (from God); these are the orders. Of these laws a man ought to be an expositor, to these he ought to submit, not to those of Masurius and Cassius.
source_reference: Discourses, What Things We Should Exchange for Other Things
